title: Quadratic total resolution space for linear-size CNFs
formal:
Do linear-size CNF formulas of constant input-clause width attain the quadratic worst-case bound on total resolution space?

Precisely, do there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge1\), positive real constants \(a,b,c\), an integer \(n_0\ge1\), and a family of unsatisfiable \(k\)-CNF formulas \((F_n)_{n\ge n_0}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_0\),
\[a n\le N(F_n)\le b n\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{TotSp}(F_n)\ge c n^2?\]
Here \(N(F)=|F|+\sum_{C\in F}|C|\) counts input clauses and literal occurrences. The total space of a resolution refutation is the maximum, over its memory configurations, of the total number of literal occurrences in the clauses simultaneously retained; \(\operatorname{TotSp}(F)\) minimizes this quantity over all general resolution refutations of \(F\).

The answer is known to be yes. This card records the resolved 2013 question and its published resolution, rather than an active open problem.
why: This question identified whether memory requirements of resolution can grow quadratically even when the inconsistent input itself has only linear size and constant-width clauses. Its affirmative resolution shows that the worst-case memory bound is a real feature of compact propositional reasoning instances, rather than an artifact of presenting an enormous formula.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Bonacina, Galesi and Thapen, FOCS 2014 and SIAM Journal on Computing 45(5) (2016), Theorem 1.1 and §5. On 16 September 2026 the published full text was read for its configuration model, central lower-bound statement and proof, fixed-density random-CNF application and linear-size conclusion. At a sufficiently large fixed density unsatisfiability holds with high probability as stated in §5; the intersection supplies the family in the original question. The mathematical parameters match the source target. This is a checked published resolution, not a newly constructed or Lean-checked proof by the reviewer.

progress.text: The survey attributes the total-space question to Alekhnovich and coauthors and states its linear-size, constant-width version as Open Problem 10.
The conference version of Total Space in Resolution establishes quadratic lower bounds for constant-width linear-size formulas.

The published journal version states Theorem 1.1 for fixed-width random CNFs and explains the resulting tight quadratic bound. Its definitions and §5 apply to the literal-occurrence total-space measure required here.

Scientifically significant, but unsuitable for the active open-problem pool because the stated existence question has a published affirmative resolution.

sentences: The original question asks whether a compact inconsistent formula can force quadratic memory use in resolution.
Input size counts clauses and literal occurrences, while total space counts all literal occurrences in clauses retained at the same time.
The clause width of the input must stay bounded by one fixed constant throughout the family.
Bonacina, Galesi and Thapen proved that suitable linear-size fixed-width formulas attain the quadratic bound.
The research question is therefore resolved and this card belongs in the inactive archive.

definitions:
A Boolean variable has value zero or one. A literal is either a variable or its negation. A clause is a finite set of literals, interpreted as their disjunction; it has no repeated literal and no complementary pair. The empty clause \(\bot\) is false. A CNF formula is a finite set of clauses interpreted as their conjunction, and is unsatisfiable when no assignment satisfies every input clause. A \(k\)-CNF has at most \(k\) literals in each input clause. This fixed bound does not restrict the width of derived clauses.

The variable universe of a proof is the set of variables occurring in its input formula. Variable names carry no cost in \(N(F)\): one can rename them consecutively. Duplicate clauses do not pad formula size because a formula is a set. The parameter \(n\) indexes the family and is within constant factors of its number of input clauses and literal occurrences as stipulated above; it is not the number of bits in a binary encoding. Counting binary variable names could add a logarithmic factor and is not the size convention of this question.

A configuration is a finite set of clauses over the input variables. A refutation is a finite sequence \(\mathcal D_0,\ldots,\mathcal D_T\), starting with \(\mathcal D_0=\varnothing\) and ending with \(\bot\in\mathcal D_T\). A step may download an input clause, erase a retained clause, or add a resolvent from two retained clauses. The resolution rule derives \(C\cup D\) from \(C\cup\{x\}\) and \(D\cup\{\neg x\}\), where \(C,D\) contain neither polarity of the pivot \(x\), and the resolvent is non-tautological. As in the original survey, weakening may also add literals to a retained clause, without introducing new variables or a tautological clause. Weakening can be removed from refutations without increasing the minimum total space. Arbitrary semantic consequence is not a permitted inference rule.

An inference adds its conclusion while its premises are still in memory. Premises can be erased in later steps. Erased input clauses may be downloaded again, and erased derived clauses must be derived again before reuse. The input formula is available read-only for downloads and is not charged until a clause is retained. There is no bound on proof length, number of downloads or running time. Refutations can share intermediate clauses and can resolve on the same variable more than once along a dependency path; no tree-like or regularity restriction is imposed. No extension variables or stronger proof rules are available.

For a configuration and a refutation define
\[\operatorname{TotSp}(\mathcal D)=\sum_{C\in\mathcal D}|C|,\qquad \operatorname{TotSp}(\pi)=\max_{0\le t\le T}\operatorname{TotSp}(\mathcal D_t),\qquad \operatorname{TotSp}(F)=\min_{\pi:F\vdash\bot}\operatorname{TotSp}(\pi).\]
The last minimum exists for every unsatisfiable formula by resolution completeness. If a variable appears in several different retained clauses, every occurrence is counted, including occurrences with different signs. The empty clause contributes zero literals. Repeated copies of the same clause need not be stored because configurations are sets.

Total space is different from clause space, which assigns cost one to each retained clause regardless of its width, and from variable space, which counts each mentioned variable only once. It also differs from the bit length of memory: literal indices, punctuation and pointers are not charged. In particular, a large width somewhere in a proof and a large clause count somewhere else do not by themselves imply a large total-space bound at any one instant.

All of \(k,a,b,c,n_0\) are fixed for the entire family and independent of \(n\). The requested lower bound holds for every refutation of every \(F_n\), including proofs of arbitrarily large length. The family need not be generated in polynomial time; the source asks for existence of fixed-width linear-size formulas, with no additional efficient-construction requirement. A probabilistic existence proof is allowed if it establishes such a family and the universal lower bound. No success probability or approximation error is part of the refutation model.

The assertion is an exact asymptotic existence statement. Its logical negation would rule out every choice of fixed constants and every such family, rather than merely refute a particular proposed family. Polynomial-size formulas in the number of variables would not alone suffice: the stated linear size and the same parameter in the quadratic lower bound must both hold.
answer_criterion: A positive answer requires a complete Lean-checked existence proof of constants and a family satisfying both the linear input-size condition and the quadratic lower bound on the total space of every general resolution refutation. A concrete computable family or a fully proved probabilistic existence argument may qualify; polynomial-time construction is not required. A negative answer would require a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation of the quantified assertion. The published affirmative result resolves the research question, but a citation to it alone is not a Lean proof. The target is exact in asymptotic order, so the default numerical tolerance does not apply. A lower bound only on clause count, only on width, only on short proofs, or only for exponentially large input formulas does not meet the target.

source_formulation.text: Open Problem 10 asks whether there are unsatisfiable CNF families with a fixed bound on input-clause width and linear input size whose minimum total resolution space is quadratic in that size parameter.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the original question; resolved by later work, with literal-occurrence size and space made explicit

context_blocks.text: Resolution certifies unsatisfiability by deriving clauses until it reaches the empty clause. Its total-space measure records the number of literal occurrences that must coexist in memory during this process, giving a closer account of clause storage than simply counting retained clauses.

Every unsatisfiable formula on \(v\) variables has a resolution refutation with at most \(v+1\) retained clauses, each of width at most \(v\). Hence the universal upper bound is \(v(v+1)\), and therefore \(O(N(F)^2)\) in the input-size convention used here. The question asks whether a compact formula can force this order of memory.

Earlier quadratic lower bounds included formulas with exponentially many wide input clauses. Such examples do not establish a quadratic lower bound relative to a linear-size fixed-width input. Keeping the input compact is the essential feature of this question.

Bonacina, Galesi and Thapen prove that, for fixed clause width at least four and fixed clause density, a random formula with linearly many clauses has, with probability tending to one, the following property: every resolution refutation contains linearly many clauses of linear width simultaneously. At a sufficiently large fixed density these formulas are also unsatisfiable with probability tending to one. Thus their published theorem supplies the requested linear-size families and quadratic total-space bound.

The same paper gives quadratic bounds for graph pigeonhole formulas and discusses further developments for random 3-CNFs. The affirmative answer to this card already follows from the fixed-width random-formula result; requiring width exactly three would be an additional specialization, not part of the original existential target.

The total-space lower bound concerns all refutations, with no cap on their length. Questions about forcing large space while still allowing short refutations, or about total space in stronger proof systems, are different targets and are not inserted into this resolved record.
